newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia to issue Eurobond to cover deficit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia to issue Eurobond to cover deficit.

text.p: Russia announced on Tuesday it planned to call for funds again soon from international capital markets with a new dollar Eurobond after its recent successful dollar and mark issues.
A brief statement from First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said the dollar bond, running for at least five years, would be managed by investment banks JP Morgan and SBC Warburg.
Russia issued a heavily oversubscribed $1 billion dollar five-year bond in November last year, and a well received two billion mark ($1.2 billion), seven-year bond in March this year.

Officials have repeatedly said there will be further borrowing this year, with a dollar Eurobond and one denominated in a currency still to be decided, but had previously said these issues would probably follow in the autumn.
But economists said plans to tap the market now had been spurred by intense budget deficit pressure.
"All the money they get now goes into paying pensions and wages -- that is what happened with the Deutschemark issue," said Florian Fenner, research analyst at Brunswick.
"They don't care how they do that, they just want to do it."
Tax revenues in the first quarter were only 60 percent of budgeted levels.
Economists said the Russian government, already the focus of domestic outrage over chronic wage and pension arrears and facing severe budget cuts this month, desperately needed the bond money.
The International Monetary Fund has effectively suspended payments of its $10 billion three-year loan this year and there are no signs that a resumption of lending is imminent.
"I would have thought they'd want the Eurobond out as quickly as possible because of the delay in IMF disbursement this year," said Charles Robertson, East European analyst at Hilfe.
Economists said Russia also hoped to capitalise on the positive tone of recent coments by IMF head Michel Camdessus and World Bank President James Wolfensohn by issuing the bond soon.
Camdessus said Russia could become an economic superpower if it pursued reforms actively, and Wolfensohn pledged $6 billion in loans to Russia over the next two years during his visit.

"I imagine they're going to be aiming at a lower yield than either of (the previous) two, as they have seemingly more enthusiastic IMF backing and top reformists in key positions in the government since the March reshuffle," Robertson said.
Russia's November 9.25 percent bond, the largest ever sovereign debut issue, was priced to yield 345 basis points over five-year U.S. Treasury notes.
Russia was rated BB- by Standard and Poor's, Ba2 by Moody's and BB+ by IBCA for the issue.
Demand for Russia's Eurobonds, and an active domestic government securities market on which foreign investors are active players have reduced Russia's dependence on the IMF as a source of funds.
Chubais said last week Russia might receive its last IMF loan this year and economic conditions allowed a transition from World Bank loans directly funding the budget to concrete investment projects.
But the presence of an IMF programme is still an important source of customers to investors in Russian paper.

Several regional governments and companies have announced plans to issue Eurobonds, and the cities of Moscow, St Petersburg and Nizhny Novgorod region were last week granted permission to issue their own bonds.
"In a year's time its not going to be big news anymore that Russia is issuing Eurobonds," Fenner said.
